title: Gaps, islands and data quality
summary: Streaks, missing numbers, and a report that tells you what's wrong with the data before your boss does.

steps.title: Gaps and islands
body: The loyalty app rewards **streaks**: consecutive days of opening the app. Rows of consecutive days are **islands**; the missing days between them are **gaps**.
The trick: subtract a row number from the date. Within an island both go up by one each row, so the difference stays **constant**:
```text
day         row_number  day - row_number
```sql
WITH t AS (
SELECT member, day,
date(day, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY member ORDER BY day) || ' days') AS grp
FROM app_logins
SELECT member, MIN(day) AS start, MAX(day) AS finish, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM t
GROUP BY member, grp;

code: SELECT day, date(day, '-' || ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day) || ' days') AS grp
SELECT MIN(day), COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY grp ORDER BY 1;
setup: CREATE TABLE app_logins (member TEXT, day TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (member, day));
CREATE TABLE invoices (no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, issued TEXT);
steps.explain: Ben's days are the 2nd, then the 4th to the 7th: two islands.

steps.title: Missing invoice numbers
prompt: Invoice numbers should have no gaps (auditors ask about every missing one). Using `LEAD`, return each gap as **gap_start** and **gap_end**: the first and last missing number.
Tables: `app_logins(member, day)` (one row per member per day they opened the app) and `invoices(no, issued)`.
solution: SELECT no, LEAD(no) OVER (ORDER BY no) AS next_no FROM invoices
SELECT no + 1 AS gap_start, next_no - 1 AS gap_end
setup: CREATE TABLE app_logins (member TEXT, day TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (member, day));
CREATE TABLE invoices (no INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, issued TEXT);
hints: Pair each number with the next one using LEAD.
A gap is where the next number is more than 1 higher.

steps.title: Data quality checks
body: Before anyone trusts a report, check the data. A **quality report** is a UNION ALL of small checks, each counting the rows that break one rule:
```sql
SELECT 'missing email' AS problem, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM members WHERE email IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'duplicate email', COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT email FROM members WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'invalid date', COUNT(*) FROM members WHERE date(joined) IS NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT 'negative points', COUNT(*) FROM members WHERE points < 0;

`date(x)` returns NULL for text that isn't a valid date, a handy validity test. Other typical checks: **orphans** (child rows whose parent is missing), out-of-range values, and totals that don't reconcile with another system. Run the report on a schedule and alert when a count isn't zero.

steps.title: The quality report
prompt: Build the quality report for the loyalty data. Return two columns, **problem** and **rows**, one row for each of these five problems:
2. `duplicate email`: number of **emails** that appear more than once
3. `invalid joined date`: members whose `joined` isn't a valid date
5. `orphan redemption`: redemptions whose member doesn't exist
Tables: `members(id, email, joined, points)` and `redemptions(id, member_id, points)`.
solution: SELECT 'missing email' AS problem, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM members WHERE email IS NULL
SELECT 'duplicate email', COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT email FROM members WHERE email IS NOT NULL GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)
SELECT 'invalid joined date', COUNT(*) FROM members WHERE date(joined) IS NULL
SELECT 'negative points', COUNT(*) FROM members WHERE points < 0
SELECT 'orphan redemption', COUNT(*) FROM redemptions AS r WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM members AS m WHERE m.id = r.member_id);
setup: CREATE TABLE members (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, joined TEXT, points INTEGER);
CREATE TABLE redemptions (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, member_id INTEGER, points INTEGER);
INSERT INTO redemptions VALUES (1,1,50),(2,4,10),(3,9,30),(4,6,5);
hints: Five SELECTs joined with UNION ALL; the column names come from the first one.
Each SELECT returns one row: a label in quotes and a COUNT(*).

steps.title: Dialect cheat sheet
body: You'll meet all of these eventually. The same intent, four spellings:
```text
intent              SQLite                   PostgreSQL                 SQL Server                     MySQL
first N rows        LIMIT n                  LIMIT n / FETCH FIRST n    TOP (n) / OFFSET..FETCH        LIMIT n
null fallback       COALESCE / IFNULL        COALESCE                   COALESCE / ISNULL              COALESCE / IFNULL
auto id             INTEGER PRIMARY KEY      GENERATED AS IDENTITY      IDENTITY(1,1)                  AUTO_INCREMENT
(AUTOINCREMENT)          (or SERIAL)
concat              a || b                   a || b, concat()           a + b, CONCAT()                CONCAT(a, b)
string length       length()                 length()                   LEN()                          CHAR_LENGTH()
upsert              ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE    ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE      MERGE                          ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
boolean             0 / 1                    true / false               BIT 0 / 1                      0 / 1 (TINYINT)
recursive CTE       WITH RECURSIVE           WITH RECURSIVE             WITH                           WITH RECURSIVE
returning rows      RETURNING                RETURNING                  OUTPUT inserted.*              (none)
quoted name         "name"                   "name"                     [name] / "name"                `name`
The core (SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, window functions, CTEs) is the same everywhere. That's the part this course spent most of its time on.

prompt: For each **orphan** redemption, return its **id**, the missing **member_id**, and its **points**. Use a LEFT JOIN anti-join.
Tables: `members(id, email, joined, points)` and `redemptions(id, member_id, points)`.
solution: LEFT JOIN members AS m ON m.id = r.member_id
